item.title: Parametric Proof-Carrying Compilation for Quantum Error-Correction
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — PC-QEC produces finite symbolic certificates proving circuit-level code distance bounds across entire parameterized code families for four syndrome-extraction schemes, verifying distance lower bound d for rotated Surface codes for all odd d≥3 in 214 s on average.

Grade 0.524 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · John Zhuoyang Ye, Jens Palsberg

Figure

The workflow translating high-level code algebra and extraction invariants via Standard, Flag, Shor, or Knill schemes into compiled circuits and verifiable Hoare-logic certificates, contrasted with cut parities distinguishing logical errors from hook errors.

Asks

How can a quantum error-correcting code family's geometric structure be turned into a finite proof that its circuit-level distance lower bound survives syndrome-extraction compilation?

But

Circuit-level fault model is restricted to single-wire Pauli faults; Shor and Knill scheme family certificates require zero edge/resource/Bell readout flips; triangular color codes yield only a certified lower bound ⌈d/3⌉.

Tools

proof-carrying compilation · fault-aware quantum Hoare logic · algebraic parity cuts · Lean 4 formalization · OCaml certificate verifier

Abstract

We present PC-QEC, a proof-carrying compilation framework for quantum error correction parameterized by both code distance and syndrome-extraction scheme. It covers all four schemes---Standard, Flag, Shor and Knill---with circuit-level distance guarantees for every legal code distance in each proved family under the declared fault and readout contracts. The circuit-level model permits single-wire Pauli faults at every operation's qubit operands, capturing data errors, readout errors and ancilla faults that propagate into multi-qubit hook errors. For each family and scheme, code-algebra proofs and fault-aware Hoare proofs compose into a finite symbolic certificate whose size is independent of code distance. We demonstrate family-wide guarantees for five code families across all four schemes. For rotated Surface code, one Standard Scheme certificate proves a distance lower bound d for every odd d≥3 and checks in 214 s on average. Lean 4 mechanizes the metatheory and exact circuit-level distances for canonical Surface, hypergraph-product (HGP) and Toric code families.

item.title: Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — PRISM transformer-based decoder matches logical error rates of integer programming decoders up to 50% of threshold across surface, color, and qLDPC codes (distances up to 24). FPGA implementation decodes distance-8 space-time blocks with 6.59 microseconds latency and 1.56 microseconds amortized time per block.

Grade 0.516 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Daniel Barter, Jacob C. Bridgeman, Chris Dawson, Terry Farrelly, Shane Fleming, Mercedes Gimeno-Segovia, Paul Hartke, Timothy Hein, Sean Howell, Gregory Hyegang Jun, Siddhartha Kamalakara, Yehua Liu, Jose M. Monsalve Diaz, Eddie Richter, Sam Roberts

Asks

Can machine-learning decoders handle erasure-dominated quantum error models accurately with real-time throughput and sub-10 microsecond latency?

Before

Integer programming decoders provide high accuracy for erasure-rich architectures but are computationally slow and unsuitable for real-time decoding.

But

Evaluated on simulated error models with Pauli and erasure errors; distance-8 limit on the specific single-FPGA real-time implementation.

Tools

Transformer neural network (PRISM) · AMD VP1902 FPGA · Fusion-based quantum computing simulations

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that combine accuracy, throughput, low latency, and scalability to large numbers of physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, erasures from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements are a dominant error mechanism, motivating decoders that remain accurate at high erasure rates. We introduce PRISM, a transformer-based machine-learning decoder designed to exploit the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. We benchmark PRISM across a wide range of fault-tolerant protocols based on surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes, with distances up to 24. Across these benchmarks, PRISM matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. We further optimize the decoder and its real-time hardware implementation to reduce latency while maintaining accuracy. Our optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA can decode logical blocks of distance 8 in both space and time, demonstrating a latency of 6.59 microseconds and an amortized decoding time of 1.56 microseconds per logical block is possible. These results show that machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

item.title: Syndrome extraction for quantum LDPC codes in silicon: Distributed entanglement and mobile ancillas
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Mapping mobile-ancilla extraction onto a node lattice shortens the mean scheduled route for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code from 350 to 153 μm and reduces logical error rate up to 50-fold, beating distributed-singlet circuits across all sampled points unless two-qubit gate and readout errors fall below 4×10−4 to 5×10−4.

Grade 0.487 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · William Chow, Jonathan Baugh

Figure

Logical error rate per round versus shuttle dephasing probability psh across three bit-flip noise ratios, comparing original CAbLECAR, CAbLECAR remapped to the authors' node lattice, and distributed singlet gadgets (teleport and GHZ).

Asks

How do distributed-entanglement syndrome-extraction circuits compare to mobile ancilla transport for bivariate-bicycle codes on a shuttling-based silicon spin-qubit architecture?

Before

CAbLECAR mobile-ancilla scheduler on its original layout, which achieved a mean Gross-code route of 350 μm and was outperformed by teleportation under frequent transport bit flips.

But

Circuit-level memory simulations, open boundary conditions, non-faulty source undetectable fraction f=0 default, 12 rounds on [[144,12,12]] Gross code.

Tools

bivariate-bicycle code simulations · singlet fabric architecture · coherent electron shuttling · BP+OSD decoding

Code. https://github.com/KNFLWNF/singlet-fabric-qldpc

Abstract

Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can reduce the number of data qubits required per logical qubit, but their checks require long-range interactions on a planar device. We develop a singlet fabric for bivariate-bicycle codes on a silicon node network. Spin singlets are generated on shuttling lanes and distributed between nodes, where local operations consume them to measure non-local stabilizers. We construct two syndrome-extraction circuits, based on distributed GHZ states and ancilla teleportation, and evaluate them using hardware-constrained schedules and circuit-level memory simulations. We compare these circuits with CAbLECAR, which transports a mobile ancilla between the data qubits of each check. Teleportation can outperform CAbLECAR on its original layout when transport includes spin flips as well as dephasing. Placing the mobile ancilla on our node lattice, however, shortens the mean scheduled route for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code from 350 to 153 μm and lowers its logical error rate up to 50-fold in the sampled bit-flip regime. Direct transport then achieves a lower logical error rate than either singlet circuit at every sampled Gross-code point. With frequent transport bit flips, the GHZ circuit overtakes direct transport once two-qubit gate and readout errors fall below about 4-5×10⁻⁴, roughly half the value assumed here. Fixing the ancilla's data-visit order reveals a trade-off between shorter routes and the correlated errors produced by ancilla faults. Source heralding improves both singlet circuits, whereas phase purification helps the GHZ circuit only above a noise-dependent crossover and worsens teleportation throughout. These results show that the physical layout and interaction order can be as consequential as the choice of extraction circuit, and that cleaner entangled resources do not necessarily produce a more reliable logical memory.

item.title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — FTQC provides an MLIR dialect with an ECC-aware type system; on the 20-qubit Pathfinder device, decoding lowered logical readout error by a factor of 3.3.

Grade 0.451 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “lattice surgery, logical qubit layout and compilation to a fault-tolerant instr…” · Narasinga Rao Miniskar, Elaine Wong, Seyong Lee, Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Jeffrey S. Vetter, Travis S. Humble

Figure

In-pipeline compile time (parse plus passes) as a function of logical qubit count n across six benchmark circuit families. Near-linear families execute in under 6 ms at n=100, while QFT scales quadratically to 100 ms at n=51.

Asks

How can a quantum compiler preserve error-correcting code information and resource constraints while lowering logical circuits to physical backends?

But

Logical error estimates use leading-order model; distillation tracks peak qubits rather than space-time volume; non-Clifford gates replaced with Clifford stand-ins in Stim; no threshold scaling shown.

Tools

MLIR and ODS · OpenQASM 3.0 · QIR · Stim and PyMatching · 20-qubit Pathfinder (ORNL)

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

item.title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Large superconducting quantum processors (107 to 156 qubits) support GHZ states passing genuine multipartite entanglement non-exclusion criteria on at most N∗=27 and N∗=24 qubits (<23% of register), whereas a 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes on its full register (N∗=12). Under a strict GME certification rule, only four of nine commercial processors succeed at any tested size.

Grade 0.418 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Sergio Hernández, Unai Aseguinolaza, David Aguirre, Marta Gili, Joseba Hernández, Guillermo Valverde, Uxue Ballarin Manso, Uxue Auzmendi, Iker Pastor, Pablo García Bringas, Ane Blázquez García, Rubén Peña, Mikel Sanz

Figure

Comparison of largest passing GHZ size N∗ against total physical qubits Ntot, alongside register utilization ratios and per-qubit GHZ error rates across nine processors.

Asks

How do commercial cloud-accessible quantum computing platforms across different hardware modalities compare when preparing genuine multipartite entangled GHZ states under standard end-user compilation?

But

Default provider compilations without error mitigation; stabilizer sample size set by ε=δ=0.10; evaluations limited to single runs or sparse binary-searched register sizes.

Tools

QuSquare benchmark suite · Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) · remote cloud-access APIs (Amazon Braket, Qiskit Runtime) · superconducting and trapped-ion QPUs

Code. https://github.com/NQUIRE-Center/Cross-Platform-Benchmarking/tree/main/GHZ-State_Generation

Abstract

Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold F=1/2. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach N^*=27 and N^*=24 qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.

item.title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Querying a 12-qubit address bucket-brigade QRAM on superconducting hardware achieves 0.969 fidelity while consuming 3.51×10−4J dynamic energy, 4.38W average dynamic power, and 64.4W peak power.

Grade 0.411 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Joao F. Doriguello, Alessandro Luongo, Harshit Verma

Asks

What is the physical energetic cost of executing a QRAM query on a superconducting processor at a target fidelity?

But

Physical simulation using superconducting gate set decomposition, multi-stage dilution refrigerator thermal photon model, and gate noise models.

Tools

metric-noise-resource framework · bucket-brigade QRAM architecture · linear-depth multiplexer QRAM · cryogenic attenuation profile optimization

Abstract

Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a 12-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of 0.969. The query consumes 3.51×10⁻⁴ J of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of 4.38 W and a peak of 64.4 W. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.

item.arxave:abstract: Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a 12-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of 0.969. The query consumes 3.51×10⁻⁴ J of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of 4.38 W and a peak of 64.4 W. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.

item.title: How wide must an eavesdropper be? Leakage of a toric-code logical bit to a strip and the Nishimori point
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Trace-distance leakage to any region A under general Pauli noise is exactly ϵA=1−2PMLfail(A). A region missing a single column yields ϵA=0, while for uniform noise a two-row strip leaks identically to a single row.

Grade 0.407 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Konstantinos Karagiannis

Figure

Adversary advantage ϵ plotted against injected bit-flip rate pinj on ibm_marrakesh (d=3 and d=5) for strip widths w=1,2,3,4. Points show hardware data decoded by model and learned attackers; curves show theoretical predictions for uniform i.i.d. noise.

Asks

How much information about a toric-code logical bit leaks to a localized spatial subregion under noise?

But

Treats single-round Pauli noise with perfect measurement (no circuit-level syndrome extraction noise). Adversary is emulated offline on d=3,5 quantum processors without a physical side-channel measurement.

Tools

Regional leakage–decoding identity · Walsh–Hadamard transfer matrix · IBM Heron processors (ibm_marrakesh, ibm_kingston) · Random-bond Ising model mapping

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computers hand pieces of each logical qubit to separate decoder modules and shared readout lines. How much does a piece reveal? We prove that for any region and any Pauli noise, including correlated noise, an observer's optimal advantage in learning a logical bit is exactly 1 - 2 P_fail, where P_fail is the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding confined to that region. Two lessons follow. Geometry, not noise, provides the protection: a region that misses a single column of the code learns exactly nothing at any noise level, while a region that spans the code is protected by noise only at impractical distances (d > 350 for one row at a 10^-3 flip rate). And width is a poor guide to risk: under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip learns exactly as little as one row, yet below threshold an eavesdropper needs a width growing only as ln d. Through the identity, the strip's operational threshold is the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, and a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix up to width 16 locates it to within a few thousandths. On two IBM Heron processors (d = 3, 5), an emulated strip adversary shows the predicted jump at width three, and non-uniform qubit errors let a trained attacker profit from the second row that uniform noise makes useless. We turn these results into design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout. Code and data are included.

item.title: Dynamical GKP codes
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Formulation of dynamical and subsystem continuous-variable GKP codes with update rules for symplectic lattices, ancestry tracking, and distance computation. Single-mode translation measurements with irrational symplectic overlap reduce to destructive homodyne detection.

Grade 0.397 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Jonathan Pelletier, Baptiste Royer

Figure

Measurement schedule for the two-mode square-hexagonal Floquet GKP code across discrete rounds, indicating two-mode translation measurements on modes 1 and 2.

Asks

How can the dynamical and Floquet error-correction framework developed for qubits be extended to continuous-variable Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codes?

But

Finite-energy GKP states require bounded displacement widths ej≤Δ; irrational-overlap reduction to homodyne detection fails in multi-mode codes when primitive vectors cannot be decomposed into a single symplectic plane (k≥2).

Tools

scaled symplectic lattices · ancestry tracking · benign error generators · Floquet measurement schedules · Diophantine approximation

Abstract

Dynamical codes protect quantum information with sequences of measurements, generalizing the stabilizer formalism of static codes. However, the dynamical formalism has been developed exclusively for qubit systems. While Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes are promising candidates for quantum computing that encode qubits in the continuous phase space of oscillators, no dynamical formalism has been developed for them. In this work, we bridge this gap and introduce dynamical GKP codes, combining continuous-variable lattice encodings with time-dependent translation measurement dynamics. To obtain the update rules and the distance of a given measurement sequence, we first generalize GKP codes to subsystem GKP codes using scaled symplectic lattices. Building on this structure, we adapt the ancestry, detector, and benign-error machinery originally developed for dynamical qubit codes. From this construction, we obtain a general and efficient method to compute the syndrome and distance of a dynamical GKP code from a persistent stabilizer lattice and a bounded inference window. We illustrate the framework with the example of the two-mode square-hexagonal Floquet GKP code. This code has reduced measurement weight compared to both the square and hexagonal GKP codes, while combining their set of logical gates, resulting in easier implementation of the full single-qubit Clifford group. Finally, we show that measurements with irrational symplectic overlap, which have no analog in discrete qubit codes, reduce to destructive homodyne detection in the single-mode case. These results extend an important qubit-code tool to continuous-variable systems and identify a new bridge between discrete stabilizer measurements and continuous homodyne detection.
